examples.problem: Use the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t).$
examples.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 3.$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}-{e}^{t}} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}+L{-{e}^{t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3 \\ L{{e}^{t}} & =\frac{1}{s-1},\,s>1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{1}{s-1} \\  & =\frac{(s-1)-(s+3)}{(s+3)(s-1)} \\  & =\frac{-4}{(s+3)(s-1)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(s+3)(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{t}}$ is defined for $s\in (1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-3,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=(1,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>1.$
